question:
A radioactive source emits **monochromatic electromagnetic radiation** of frequency $\nu$ (constant in time) such that $h\nu>\phi$ for a given metal cathode of a photoelectric cell. The geometry is fixed so that the **photon flux (hence intensity) incident on the cathode is directly proportional to the source activity** $A(t)$.

The radiation is initially **unpolarized** and is passed successively through an ideal polarizer $P$ and an ideal analyzer $A$ whose transmission axis makes an angle $\theta$ with that of $P$. The photoelectric cell is operated in the **saturation region**, so the saturation photocurrent is proportional to the incident intensity.

At $t=0$, with $\theta=0^{\circ}$, the saturation current is $I_1=8\,\mu\text{A}$.

At $t=10\,\text{min}$, the analyzer is rotated to $\theta=60^{\circ}$ and the saturation current becomes $I_2=1\,\mu\text{A}$.

Assuming exponential decay $A(t)=A_0\,2^{-t/T_{1/2}}$, determine the half-life $T_{1/2}$ of the radioactive source.
